clue.text: Eggs on toast?

definitions.meaning: to egg someone on is to urge or encourage them, as a crowd shouting approval does
a toast is a drink raised to someone's health, with the familiar word said as glasses clink

explanation.surface: A breakfast question about what goes on a slice of toast.
explanation.definitionFit: Encouraging shouts and the word said when drinking a health are both the same exclamation.

clue.text: They're said to be wholly delicious

definitions.text: They're said to be wholly delicious

parts.words: They're said to be wholly delicious
parts.note: 'wholly' heard as 'holey': these griddle cakes are riddled with holes on top, and much loved toasted with butter

explanation.surface: A description of some much-praised treat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wholly' sounds like 'holey', which is the real joke: the British teatime cake is full of holes. 'Said to be' signals the sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: These soft griddle cakes are famous for their holey tops and are a teatime favourite.

clue.text: Dr Livingstone I presume? Find out that it's right

parts.note: to explore is to investigate and find out about

explanation.surface: A nod to the famous greeting, asking whether the guess is correct.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the famous greeting Stanley gave the Scottish missionary-traveller in Africa, standing for the man himself.
explanation.definitionFit: David Livingstone was a celebrated traveller who charted unknown parts of Africa.

clue.text: In Wales it's a bit unusual

definitions.meaning: Welsh rarebit is cheese on toast, so in Wales this word comes before 'bit'

explanation.surface: A remark that something is somewhat uncommon in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: Welsh rarebit is a dish of melted cheese on toast; the clue splits it as a word plus 'bit'.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncommon and seldom seen; and the first part of the name of the Welsh cheese dish.

clue.text: The sole tabu, however it's unconditional

indicators.note: read as 'how-ever', in whatever way they are arranged, so the letters of the words sole and tabu are mixed

explanation.surface: A comment that some prohibition on a fish is total whatever happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'however' is the anagram signal: the eight letters of SOLE TABU are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Something total and without limits or conditions is complete in every respect.

clue.text: Cowardly piece of work

parts.note: read 'Cowardly' as by Noel Coward: a work written by the playwright, here a comedy about a ghostly wife

explanation.surface: A scornful description of a timid, nasty person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cowardly' means belonging to Noel Coward, the English playwright, and 'piece of work' is one of his plays, his 1941 comedy about a séance.
explanation.definitionFit: This 1941 comedy, about a medium who summons a dead wife, is one of Noel Coward's best-known plays.

clue.text: Space made for Latin poet

indicators.note: here 'made for' a new form: the letters of a word for emptiness are reshaped

parts.note: a void is an empty space

explanation.surface: Room being cleared for a Roman writer.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram is of a synonym, not the printed word: 'Space' gives VOID, and 'made' signals that its letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Publius Ovidius Naso, author of the Metamorphoses, was a poet of ancient Rome.

clue.text: Relax, as slackers do

definitions.meaning: to relax is to wind down and take it easy
a rope or cable slackens as it comes off its reel

explanation.surface: Advice to take it easy, like idlers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slackers' looks like lazy people, but think of ropes going slack as they are let out from a drum.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking it easy, or a cable loosening off a spool: both mean easing off tension.

clue.text: A nurse arriving at the right time may still cause anger

parts.note: EN stands for Enrolled Nurse
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A punctual nurse might still annoy someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arriving at' just joins the nurse to the rest; 'the right time' splits into R and AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: To make someone furious is to incense them.

clue.text: No-one on these can afford supper

definitions.text: No-one on these can afford supper

parts.words: No-one on these can afford supper
parts.note: being 'on one's' tops of shoes, worn through to the soles, means being broke, too poor to pay for an evening meal

explanation.surface: A remark that people in certain circumstances cannot pay for an evening meal.
explanation.walkthrough: To be 'on your uppers' is a British idiom for being penniless; the answer is also an anagram of 'supper', a bonus nod.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoe tops left once the soles wear out; being down to them means having no money.

clue.text: How cavalier, to lose something so important

definitions.text: How cavalier, to lose something so important

parts.words: How cavalier, to lose something so important
parts.note: the Cavaliers were the Royalist side defeated by Parliament in the 1640s conflict in England

explanation.surface: A rebuke for someone carelessly losing something vital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cavalier' looks like an adjective meaning careless, but it is a Royalist of the English war of the 1640s, which the Cavaliers lost.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royalist Cavaliers fought and lost England's internal war against Parliament's Roundheads.

clue.text: Our time-frame may be different from Julian's

definitions.text: Our time-frame may be different from Julian's

parts.words: Our time-frame may be different from Julian's
parts.note: the Julian system of reckoning dates, from Julius Caesar, differs from the Gregorian system used today

explanation.surface: Someone's schedule doesn't match their friend Julian's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Julian' looks like a person's name, but refers to Julius Caesar's dating system, replaced by the Gregorian one we use.
explanation.definitionFit: The twelve months from January to December as fixed by the dating system, which differs between Gregorian and Julian reckoning.

clue.text: Expression of disdain one can bear

definitions.meaning: A. A. Milne's honey-loving teddy is a bear one is fond of

explanation.surface: Showing contempt for something tolerable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bear' looks like a verb meaning tolerate, but it is the animal: Winnie-the-Pooh, the bear in A. A. Milne's stories.
explanation.definitionFit: A scornful exclamation, and the name of A. A. Milne's famous toy animal.

clue.text: A schoolgirl crush on a Turk

parts.note: a pash is old British slang for a schoolgirl infatuation

explanation.surface: A girl at school falls for a man from Turkey.
explanation.walkthrough: PASH is dated British school slang for an infatuation, short for passion.
explanation.definitionFit: A pasha was a high-ranking official in the Ottoman Empire, so a Turkish dignitary.

clue.text: The drawback of first saying nothing and giggling

indicators.note: the clue says to take what comes first in each of the following words

explanation.surface: The trouble with keeping quiet then laughing.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden problem or obstacle is a downside to a plan.

clue.text: Allude to possibility of its going up or down

indicators.text: possibility of its going up or down
indicators.note: in a down clue the word reads the same whether taken upwards or downwards, so it is a palindrome

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Mentioning that something might rise or fall.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is the word itself: being a palindrome, it can be read up or down the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: To mention or point to something is to make reference to it.

clue.text: At school, mum was called alma

definitions.text: At school, mum was called alma

parts.words: At school, mum was called alma
parts.note: Latin for mother, used as public-school slang for one's mother, and half of the phrase for one's old school

explanation.surface: A pupil's mother had the name Alma.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alma' looks like the mother's name, but alma mater ('nourishing mother') is the phrase for one's old school, and the second word was British public-school slang for mum.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for mother, used jokingly by British schoolboys, and the second half of the phrase for one's old college.

clue.text: It's the main thing, the world over

definitions.text: It's the main thing, the world over

parts.words: It's the main thing, the world over
parts.note: 'the main' is a poetic term for the ocean, and these waters span the globe

explanation.surface: A claim that something is the most important thing everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'main' looks like 'principal', but the main is an old word for the open ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional phrase for all the world's oceans.

clue.text: A reminder for those who are late

definitions.text: A reminder for those who are late

parts.words: A reminder for those who are late
parts.note: 'the late' are the dead, so this is something put up to recall those who have died

explanation.surface: A nudge sent to people who keep arriving late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'late' looks like tardy, but means deceased.
explanation.definitionFit: A monument erected to commemorate those who have died.

clue.text: In the past, in a manner of speaking?

definitions.meaning: read literally, the phrase says 'as it was', describing a past state
a stock phrase meaning so to speak

explanation.surface: Wondering whether an old remark was only figurative.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom meaning 'so to speak', which read word by word describes how things once were.

clue.text: See Linda when big story breaks

indicators.note: the letters of see Linda when break apart and form something new, as news breaks

explanation.surface: Linda can be seen when a major scandal comes out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaks' is the anagram signal, apt because big stories break.
explanation.definitionFit: The top item in the news, a major report given prominence.

clue.text: In Damascus to marry veiled is the tradition

indicators.note: veiled means covered, so the answer sits concealed within the words Damascus to marry

explanation.surface: In Syria's capital, a veiled bride follows tradition.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across 'damasCUS TO Marry'; 'veiled' signals it is concealed there.
explanation.definitionFit: An established practice or convention handed down in a society.

clue.text: Touch on commercial link

parts.note: an ad is a commercial or advertisement
to join is to link

explanation.surface: Briefly mentioning an advertising tie-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Touch on' looks like a phrase meaning mention; only 'Touch' is the definition, in the sense of being next to.
explanation.definitionFit: Two things that touch are next to each other, sharing a border.

clue.text: What you are speaking is Dutch? No, Pakistani

definitions.note: the clue's adjective stands for the national language of Pakistan

parts.note: U is text-speak for you
R is text-speak for are

explanation.surface: Someone asks if the language heard is Dutch, and is told it is Pakistani.
explanation.walkthrough: U and R stand for 'you are' as in texting; the definition means the language of Pakistan.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the national language of Pakistan.

clue.text: Transport hitch for bridesmaids?

definitions.meaning: the long trailing part of a bridal gown, which bridesmaids hold up

explanation.surface: A travel problem for a wedding party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hitch' looks like a problem, but the bridesmaids' job is to carry the bride's trailing gown.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway service; and the extended back of a wedding dress.

clue.text: There's some drink left

definitions.meaning: the left-hand side of a ship facing forward

explanation.surface: A little alcohol remains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' looks like 'remaining', but it is the nautical left side.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortified Portuguese wine, and a ship's left-hand side.

clue.text: Not even a little mention of the dead?

parts.note: O, a zero, stands for nothing
a bit is a small amount

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the deceased got any mention at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not even a little' becomes O plus BIT, a zero amount; the answer is the short word for a death notice.
explanation.definitionFit: A notice in a newspaper recording someone's death and life.

clue.text: Acts to catch the bird — 200 years too late!

definitions.text: Acts to catch the bird — 200 years too late!

parts.words: Acts to catch the bird — 200 years too late!
parts.note: two acts, or 'does' twice, make up the name of a flightless Mauritius bird wiped out in the seventeenth century

explanation.surface: People trying to catch a bird that died out centuries ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Acts' gives DO and DO; the bird died out in the 1600s, so any attempt to catch it is far too late.
explanation.definitionFit: A flightless bird of Mauritius, extinct since the late 1600s.

clue.text: Without a doubt Lear could be worried

indicators.note: suggests the letters might be put together in another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's king is surely anxious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without a doubt' looks like 'certainly', but 'Without' says take the A away: rearrange DOUBT LEAR without A.
explanation.definitionFit: Being anxious or uneasy is being disturbed.

clue.text: Moving explanation for crime?

explanation.surface: A touching account of why someone broke the law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving' looks like 'touching', but means producing motion.
explanation.definitionFit: Producing movement, and the reason behind a criminal act.

clue.text: The minister a Conservative is threatening

parts.note: a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A government minister and a Tory are being menacing.
explanation.definitionFit: Menacing and intimidating is a formal word for threatening.

clue.text: Shepherd's helper may be rough

parts.note: a sheepdog breed whose long-haired variety is called 'rough', like Lassie

explanation.surface: A farmhand who assists with the flock can be coarse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rough' looks like 'coarse', but the long-coated variety of this Scottish sheepdog is called the rough one.
explanation.definitionFit: This Scottish sheepdog breed herds flocks, and its long-coated form is called rough.
